div.p: In this ongoing research, we investigate the mathematical properties of the scheduling theory and the real-time calculus and their relationship to each other.
Index Terms-real-time analysis, scheduling theory, real-time calculus, network calculus.

Much work has been published to analyze the real-time behaviour of any real-time system, e.g. [1], [6], [8], [10]. However, the approach has some limitations considering the behaviour of network processors. These components of the internet became popular in the late 1990s. However, an adaption of the network calculus [2], [7], [11] used in the performance analysis of internet traffic, the real-time calculus [2] was developed. Based on real-time calculus, the modular performance analysis for real-time systems allows the verification of distributed systems [7], [11]. On the other hand, in scheduling theory, Tindell's [10] and Richter's [8] work extends the classical approach of Lehozky [6] to analyze data dependencies in real-time systems. Therefore in a few papers, both approaches are compared empirically. The conclusion was that in some different scenarios, the results differ. In some cases, Richter's event-stream interfaces give tighter results and in others, the modular-performance analysis. However, the authors of the two papers do not present a theoretical explanation for these observations. This work claims to investigate the mathematical foundations of signal theory as a toolbox for real-time analysis. As we have shown in [9], it is possible to describe the request of any event in a real-time system with Dirac pulses. Using this approach allows the introduction of one equation to express any scheduling theory. Dirac pulses are mathematical objects behind classical functions called distributions. A distribution is some general function. The main focus of our work is to investigate if we describe bounds as distributions are it possible to unify scheduling theory and real-time calculus. In this draft, we concentrate on the response time analysis as the first step. div.p: The question now is, is there any relationship between these two equations? Note that α(t) is the workload of all tasks while β(t) is the capacity of the computational resource, e.g. a processor. The modular performance analysis is now based on this basic assumption and combines min-plus and max-plus de-convolution and convolution to compute the performance characteristics of a distributed system.

In real-time scheduling theory in task systems with static scheduling, the worst-case scenario occurs if all tasks start synchronous at the beginning of a hyper period of all tasks. However, this assumption is not valid anymore if the task set contains job requests with a given offset or the worst-case execution time differs as given in multi-frame task sets. In such a case, we can compute the response time of any job, and then we select the maximum. Let us have a closer look at equation (1). By having this in mind, we now need to bring together the operations supremum, infimum and maximum, minimum. Consider Figure 1a.: The response time analysis could be shown to be a root search on a saw function. However, if the processor is idle, the saw function becomes negative, as shown in Figure 1b. However, no processor exists which can work on future workload. As a consequence, in reality, the saw function can never become negative. Performing a maximum search over a sliding window solves this problem. The result is shown in Figure 1c by the red line. The computational operation in network calculus is the max-plus deconvolution and other operations from max-and min-plus algebra. The main mathematical property of a function is that every domain's value maps to exactly one value in the codomain. Let us consider Figure 1a. and Figure 1b. to explain this. We define one bound as an upper and one bound as a lower Heaviside function. It is easy to find a maximum or minimum because all intervals are given by subtraction a part of the set, and the result is mathematically correct because we assume a bound as distribution. Doing this has a few advantages compared to traditional techniques in real-time analysis. First, each bound function has a derivate, which is just a sum of Dirac deltas. As a result, we can apply calculus to real-time analysis. Second, assuming this derivate as a mathematical description for the term event, we can compute events in future work. The third point is that we can compute the number of events if a sequence of events is bounded. Note that the floor and ceil function only consider an infinite sequence of events, and we always have to add the operators minimum and maximum to bound the number independently from the timing occurrence. We hope in the ongoing research to show that it is possible to substitute the main contributions in realtime scheduling theory, as the demand bound test, general multiframe tasks and offset based analysis for any static or dynamic scheduling policy, by a straightforward approach. Additionally, we will show in regular papers that we can combine the advantages of the real-time calculus with the advantages of the real-time scheduling theory, replacing both approaches with a more general mathematically toolbox that includes the former approaches.
